av_event.line_text: Weekends, er... fishing, mostly. Or the park with Ruby. She's eight, Kayleigh's daughter.
av_event.what: A young girl in pyjamas walks into the frame behind Dean, picks up the pink cushion from the grey settee and walks back out of shot. Dean doesn't turn round and carries on talking.

text:
A: Hi, can you hear me okay?
B: Yeah, hiya. Dean.
A: Daniel, from Worthing. Sorry, I said on the form you looked like you were watching the football.
B: [laughs] Ar, I probably was. The telly's always on at ours.
A: Who do you support? I'm guessing from the shirt.
B: West Brom. You?
A: Brighton. I think I was at the Amex the last time we played you.
B: Ar, we probably lost, then.
A: I won't say. What do you do for work?
B: Press operator, in Wednesbury. You?
A: Trade counter at a builders' merchant. Half six starts, and Saturdays as well. I'm knackered by Friday.
B: Half six. I'm on lates this week. I'd still be asleep.
A: Lucky. Do you like it?
B: Yeah, it's alright. I sort of fell into it, if I'm honest. Me mate's dad got me in at nineteen and I just never left. Same with most things, really, do you know what I mean.
A: Yeah, I do, actually. I started a history degree, dropped out, and then sort of drifted into the counter job. Twelve years later I'm still there. I'm doing an Open University module now, trying to go back to it.
B: That's good, that. I'd never do that. I weren't any good at school.
A: I wasn't great either, honestly. You just pick the bits you like.
B: Ar. What bits do you like?
A: Ordinary people, sort of. How they actually lived. I went to Ypres with my dad, and since then I've been looking into my great-grandfather. He was a farm labourer in Sussex, and nobody wrote anything down about him.
B: Me dad's side's been in Tipton forever. Chain making, me nan said.
A: Really? That's exactly the sort of thing I'd love to know about. Do you know which works?
B: Er, no. Me nan would've. She's gone now.
A: Ah. Sorry.
B: You're alright.
A: What do you get up to at the weekends?
B: Weekends, er... fishing, mostly. Or the park with Ruby. She's eight, Kayleigh's daughter.
A: Nice. My niece is about that age. She was in a school play last week. She was a carrot.
B: [laughs] A carrot.
A: She had one line. She said it really loud, though.
B: That's the main thing. Ruby was a sheep in hers. Didn't say nothing, just stood there.
A: Do you still play any football yourself?
B: Not now. Did a bit of five-a-side in me twenties, then sort of drifted off it.
A: I've got a Wednesday lot, old school mates. Mostly we just run about and go to the pub after.
B: Ar, that's the bit I miss. The pub after.
A: You should find a group up your way. There's always someone short a—
